topics.title: Introduction to Business Risk and Financial Risk
explain: Financial management aims to maximize firm value by actively managing risks.
Business risk is the uncertainty surrounding daily operations and future operating income (EBIT).
Financial risk is the extra risk placed on equity shareholders due to using fixed-cost debt financing.
Companies issuing more debt carry higher financial risk than firms funded purely by equity.
topics.example: A retail shop faces business risk if customer footfall drops, and adds financial risk if it takes a bank loan with fixed monthly interest.
remember: Business risk relates to operational fixed costs and EBIT uncertainty.
Financial risk relates to debt financing and fixed interest obligations.
mistakes: Treating business risk and financial risk as the same thing instead of separating operations from financing.

quiz.q: Business risk refers to uncertainty regarding which financial metric?
quiz.why: Business risk reflects uncertainty in operating income (EBIT) arising from business operations.

quiz.q: Financial risk arises primarily due to the use of:
quiz.why: Financial risk stems from fixed financial charges associated with debt financing.

topics.title: Meaning and Types of Leverage
explain: Leverage represents the power or influence of one financial variable over another related variable.
It measures how a percentage change in variable X affects variable Y.
Operating leverage connects Sales to EBIT and reflects business risk.
Financial leverage connects EBIT to Earnings Per Share (EPS) and reflects financial risk.
Combined leverage connects Sales directly to EPS and reflects total risk.
topics.example: If a 10% increase in sales leads to a 20% increase in EBIT, operating leverage is magnifying the result.
remember: Operating Leverage = Sales to EBIT relationship.
Financial Leverage = EBIT to EPS relationship.
Combined Leverage = Sales to EPS relationship.
mistakes: Confusing which leverage measures which specific risk category.

quiz.q: Which type of leverage measures the relationship between EBIT and EPS?
quiz.why: Financial leverage measures how changes in operating income impact earnings per share.

quiz.q: Which leverage indicates the total risk of a business?
quiz.why: Combined leverage integrates both business and financial risks to show total risk.

topics.title: Operating Leverage and Degree of Operating Leverage (DOL)
explain: Operating leverage occurs when a firm employs assets carrying fixed operating costs.
Fixed costs remain constant, causing EBIT to change disproportionately when sales volume changes.
Degree of Operating Leverage (DOL) = Percentage Change in EBIT / Percentage Change in Sales.
At a specific output level, DOL can also be calculated as Contribution / EBIT.
If fixed costs are zero, DOL equals 1, meaning no operating leverage exists.
topics.example: A firm has ₹30,000 contribution and ₹25,000 fixed costs, giving ₹5,000 EBIT. Its DOL is 30,000 / 5,000 = 6.
remember: DOL can never be between 0 and 1; it is 0, negative, or 1 and above.
mistakes: Calculating DOL as EBIT / Contribution instead of Contribution / EBIT.

quiz.q: How is the Degree of Operating Leverage (DOL) calculated at a given output level?
quiz.why: DOL at a given point is computed as Contribution divided by EBIT.

quiz.q: If a firm has no fixed operating costs, its DOL will be:
quiz.why: Without fixed costs, Contribution equals EBIT, making DOL equal to 1.

topics.title: Break-Even Analysis and Margin of Safety in Relation to Operating Leverage
explain: Break-Even Point (BEP) is the sales volume where total sales revenue equals total costs (EBIT is zero).
Higher fixed operating costs increase both the break-even point and the degree of operating leverage.
Margin of Safety (MOS) shows how much sales can drop before reaching BEP: MOS = (Sales - BEP Sales) / Sales.
Operating leverage is the exact mathematical inverse of Margin of Safety: DOL = 1 / MOS.
A high Margin of Safety indicates low business risk and low Operating Leverage.

flow.title: Link Between Fixed Cost, BEP, and DOL

topics.example: If a company's Margin of Safety is 0.25 (25%), its Degree of Operating Leverage is 1 / 0.25 = 4.
remember: DOL = 1 / Margin of Safety (expressed as a decimal ratio).
High MOS = Low DOL = Low Business Risk.
mistakes: Assuming Margin of Safety and Operating Leverage move in the same direction when they are inversely related.

quiz.q: What is the mathematical relationship between DOL and Margin of Safety (MOS)?
quiz.why: DOL is inversely proportional to MOS, expressed as DOL = 1 / MOS.

quiz.q: When a firm operates with a high Margin of Safety, its Operating Leverage is:
quiz.why: A high Margin of Safety means sales are far above break-even, resulting in low operating leverage.

topics.title: Financial Leverage, DFL, Trading on Equity, and Double-Edged Sword
explain: Financial leverage (FL) uses fixed-cost capital (debt/preference shares) to magnify changes in EPS relative to EBIT.
Degree of Financial Leverage (DFL) = % Change in EPS / % Change in EBIT, or EBIT / EBT (without preference dividends).
When preference shares exist, DFL = EBIT / [EBIT - Interest - (Preference Dividend / (1 - Tax Rate))].
Trading on equity means employing high fixed-cost debt relative to equity to boost shareholder returns.
FL is a double-edged sword: if ROI > Interest, EPS rises (favourable); if ROI < Interest, EPS crashes (unfavourable).
topics.example: A firm earns 25% ROI while paying 15% interest on debt, generating a 10% surplus return directly for equity shareholders.
remember: DFL = EBIT / EBT (when no preference dividend exists).
Favourable FL occurs when ROI > Cost of Debt (Interest).
mistakes: Forgetting to divide Preference Dividend by (1 - Tax Rate) when computing DFL with preference capital.

quiz.q: In the absence of preference dividends, DFL is calculated as:
quiz.why: DFL is computed as EBIT divided by Earnings Before Tax (EBT).

quiz.q: Financial leverage is referred to as a 'double-edged sword' because:
o: It cuts operating costs in half
It increases EPS when ROI > Interest but severely reduces EPS when ROI < Interest
It doubles tax liabilities during high revenue periods
quiz.why: Financial leverage amplifies gains when earnings are high, but magnifies losses when earnings fall below debt costs.

topics.title: Combined Leverage and Degree of Combined Leverage (DCL)
explain: Combined leverage measures total business risk by combining operating and financial leverage.
Combined Leverage (CL) = Operating Leverage (OL) × Financial Leverage (FL).
Degree of Combined Leverage (DCL) = % Change in EPS / % Change in Sales, or Contribution / EBT.
DCL indicates how much EPS will fluctuate for a given percentage change in sales volume.
The ideal corporate risk strategy is Low Operating Leverage combined with High Financial Leverage.

flow.title: Combined Leverage Magnification Process
steps: Combined Leverage Directly Connects Sales to EPS

topics.example: If DOL is 2 and DFL is 3, DCL is 2 × 3 = 6. A 10% increase in sales will increase EPS by 60%.
remember: High DOL + High DFL is a very risky combination.
mistakes: Adding DOL and DFL together instead of multiplying them to find Combined Leverage.

quiz.q: How is the Degree of Combined Leverage (DCL) computed using DOL and DFL?
quiz.why: Combined leverage is the product of operating leverage and financial leverage.

quiz.q: In terms of profitability statement components, DCL equals:
quiz.why: DCL is derived as (Contribution / EBIT) × (EBIT / EBT) = Contribution / EBT.
